meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is plenty of time to sleep in the grave'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Shakespeare. It's a reworded version of Benjamin Franklin's proverb, "There will be sleeping enough in the Grave."

answer.label: Not William Shakespeare — a paraphrase of Benjamin Franklin
answer.authorDates: 1706–1790 · American statesman, printer & author of Poor Richard’s Almanack
answer.sourceLine: This exact wording appears in no play, poem, or sonnet of Shakespeare’s. It is a modernized paraphrase of Benjamin Franklin’s proverb — “There will be sleeping enough in the Grave” — from Poor Richard’s Almanack. The idea is Franklin’s; the smoothed “plenty of time to sleep in the grave” phrasing is a later rewording that circulates online under Shakespeare’s name.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: “There will be sleeping enough in the Grave.”

source.excerpt: How much more than is necessary do we spend in sleep, forgetting that The sleeping Fox catches no Poultry, and that There will be sleeping enough in the Grave, as Poor Richard says.
trail: The line is passed around as Shakespeare on aggregators such as Goodreads, but with no play, act, or scene ever cited.
The genuine proverb is Franklin’s: Wikiquote’s Poor Richard’s Almanack records “There will be sleeping enough in the Grave” (1758) and the earlier “in the grave will be sleeping enough” (1741).
Franklin wove the maxim into the 1758 preface known as The Way to Wealth, alongside “The sleeping Fox catches no Poultry.”
source.excerptNote: From Franklin’s 1758 preface later titled The Way to Wealth. An earlier 1741 almanac carries the kindred line “Up, Sluggard, and waste not life; in the grave will be sleeping enough.” Neither reads “There is plenty of time to sleep in the grave” — that is a later paraphrase.

sourceLink.text: Franklin’s “Poor Richard Improved,” 1758, at Founders Online

source.rightsNote: Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanack (1733–1758) is centuries old and firmly in the public domain in the United States. The popular “plenty of time to sleep in the grave” wording is an anonymous modern paraphrase of that public-domain proverb and carries no separate protectable authorship.

author.name: Benjamin Franklin
author.heading: About the real author
author.metaLine: 1706–1790 · American statesman, printer & author of Poor Richard's Almanack
author.bio: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, scientist, diplomat and Founding Father whose Poor Richard’s Almanack (published annually 1733–1758) coined or popularized dozens of enduring English proverbs. His maxims prizing industry over idleness — “Early to bed and early to rise,” “The sleeping Fox catches no Poultry” — include the line about sleeping enough in the grave that today drifts, reworded, onto Shakespeare.

misattribution.heading: How Shakespeare got the credit
misattribution.intro: A feel-good, clever line with no citation is the classic profile of a Shakespeare misattribution — and this one has a real, older author hiding behind it.

items.why: Quote aggregators like Goodreads and AZQuotes pin it on Shakespeare, but never name a play, scene, or line — and it appears in none of his works.

“There is plenty of time to sleep in the grave” is a modern smoothing; Franklin’s documented forms are “There will be sleeping enough in the Grave” (1758) and “in the grave will be sleeping enough” (1741).

misattribution.truthLine: The thought — and the memorable phrasing — belong to Benjamin Franklin’s Poor Richard’s Almanack, not to Shakespeare.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Franklin’s maxim is a hustle-culture slogan two centuries early: don’t squander waking life on sleep, because death brings all the rest you’ll ever need. It sat among the thrift-and-industry proverbs Franklin assembled into his 1758 preface, The Way to Wealth — one of the most reprinted texts of early America.
Stripped of Franklin’s name and lightly reworded, the line reads as timeless aphorism, which is exactly why it gravitates to Shakespeare, the internet’s default author for any clever orphaned quote.
